World.title: Kazakhstan-EAEU trade turnover hits $30 billion in 2025 - vice minister
World.content:
Photo: Official information resource of the Prime Minister of the Republic of Kazakhstan

ASTANA, Kazakhstan, May 28. Kazakhstan's trade turnover with the countries of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) by the end of 2025 amounted to almost $31 billion, and with the CIS countries - about $38 billion, Vice Minister of National Economy of Kazakhstan Asan Darbayev said at the Eurasian Economic Forum, Trend reports.

According to him, the region's economic interconnectedness is strengthening amid the transformation of the global economy, the restructuring of production chains, and growing competition for technology, investment, and human capital.

Darbayev noted that from 2020 through 2024, industrial production in the region grew by 15%, while agricultural output increased by 10%, adding another 4-6% last year.

"The resilience of our countries directly depends on the ability to effectively pool resources, infrastructure, and expertise," he emphasized.

The vice minister announced that the new joint action plan between the EAEU and the CIS for 2026–2030, which will be signed at the forum, will be the next stage in deepening cooperation and strengthening integration processes.

He pointed out that the implementation of digital interaction and logistics solutions will reduce customs clearance times on EAEU and CIS routes by 20–25% in the coming years.

According to Darbayev, special attention is being paid to the development of transport and logistics infrastructure. The volume of cargo transported along the Middle Corridor has increased more than fivefold over the past seven years, from 800,000 tons to 4.5 million tons.

By 2030, the corridor's traffic volume is planned to increase to 10 million tons per year, including approximately 500,000 containers, almost double current levels.

"The competitiveness of countries is increasingly determined by their level of digital development. The digital economy already accounts for over 15% of global GDP," he noted, emphasizing the priority of digitalization in the integration agenda.

Darbayev added that Kazakhstan is actively modernizing the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, expanding its railway infrastructure, and strengthening the country's transit potential as a key Eurasian logistics hub.

He also emphasized the importance of agricultural cooperation, which is creating a unified space for food security in the region, as well as the development of financial and migration services, which require closer coordination between the EAEU and CIS countries.

World.title: 'Those guys are gonna disappear': ICAC reveals 'Pink Ladies' texts
World.content:
Messages obtained by the NSW corruption watchdog have revealed discussions by a group of long-time Sydney local government officials about plans to secure senior positions for themselves and friends at City of Parramatta Council.

Angela Jones-Blayney was hired as executive director of city engagement and experience at the council in 2023, a few months after Gail Connolly was hired as CEO.

Both women along, with Roxanne Thornton, are being investigated by the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) for subverting hiring processes to benefit friends and associates.

Ms Jones-Blayney told the commission she knew Ms Connolly for nearly 30 years, since they both worked at the City of Sydney.

Outside of work, both women travelled together, attended "Pink Ladies" gatherings and went to netball games.

'I'm your number one fan'

Ms Jones-Blayney also relied on Ms Connolly's help when she was leaving Ryde Council in 2022.

When asked by counsel assisting Joanna Davidson SC if she viewed this help as an "expression of friendship", she said it was a "professional support mechanism".

Ms Davidson produced messages where Ms Jones-Blayney referred to Ms Connolly as a "beautiful friend".

In one message, Ms Connolly invited her to share a bed on a trip to Canberra saying: "You'll have to share a king bed with me if you wanna come, we're all sharing a room."

Another message sent from Ms Jones-Blayney to Ms Connolly read: "You are a f***ing legend and I'm so proud of you, and I don't know anyone in our industry that would have had the absolute strength and fortitude to have done what you've done. I admire and respect you enormously." Ms Connolly texted her back: "I'm hoping my plans work out and we can work together again sooner rather than later."

When Ms Connolly got the appointment at Parramatta council, a congratulatory message from Ms Jones-Blayney read: "You already know I'm your number one fan and rightly so, I truly admire and respect you and would walk over hot coals for you."

After presenting those messages and more to Ms Jones-Blayney, she said she and Ms Connolly were indeed "great friends".

'Those guys are gonna disappear'

The commission was shown another thread of text messages between Ms Jones-Blayney, Ms Thornton and Ms Connolly, where the three women were already discussing their plans for Parramatta council, well before Ms Jones-Blayney or Ms Thornton were hired.

On the same day Ms Connolly was offered the top job, Ms Jones-Blayney sent a message saying: "Now Roxy, you and I need to work out who we need to knock off so we can work with the rockstar again."

When asked by Ms Davidson what she meant by that, Ms Jones-Blayney said: "I don't believe that I meant that in a literal sense."

In one text message, Ms Connolly said she "can't wait to meet Bernadette and Bryan".

She was referring to then acting CEO Bryan Hynes and Bernadette Cavanagh, who led the people and culture department at the council.

Three women are being investigated by ICAC for subverting hiring processes to benefit themselves and friends. (ABC News: Warwick Ford)

Ms Cavanagh had raised concerns about the negotiating of Ms Connolly's contract, which exceeded the $500,000 per annum salary approved by a council resolution.

She refused to produce a contract and advised then-Lord Mayor Donna Davis to go back to the council chamber for approval.

Ms Cavanagh was eventually sidelined and Ms Connolly's appointment went ahead.

Ms Jones-Blayney fired back to the group thread: "Bloody idiots."

"I actually can't believe how stupid they are or that they deliriously think they can get away with it," she texted.

" Those guys are gonna disappear into a big blackhole never to be seen again. "

When asked what she meant by that, Ms Jones-Blayney said: "I can't specifically recall what I'm thinking of there."

She also told the commission she never met Ms Cavanagh or Mr Hynes.

'Stack it with our good people!'

Ms Connolly (left), heart-reacted Ms Jones-Blayney's (right) text stating council could be stacked with "our good people". (Supplied)

In another message, Ms Jones-Blayney described Ms Cavanagh as "a nightmare" and an "off-the-Richter-scale alpha female who has Bryan wrapped around her little fingers. They're all shit scared of her".

She told the ICAC information was passed on to her by someone she knew who worked at Parramatta council.

Another message from Ms Jones-Blayney to Ms Connolly said: "If Parramatta is as dysfunctional as the recruiter says, we can wipe their shit out and stack it with our good people."

Ms Connolly heart-reacted the message.

Ms Cavanagh's employment was terminated on May 26, 2023 — only eight weeks after Ms Connolly got the top job.

Mr Hynes left in October that same year.

Ms Jones-Blayney will continue giving evidence on Friday.

World.title: AFP defends public arrest of Ben Roberts-Smith
World.content:
Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett has pushed back on criticism surrounding the public arrest of former soldier Ben Roberts-Smith during a parliamentary hearing.

Roberts-Smith was arrested at Sydney Airport on April 7 after travelling from Brisbane with his family, and charged with five counts of the war crime of murder.

The Victoria Cross recipient is currently on bail and has said he categorically denies all of the allegations.

The circumstances of the arrest prompted some concerns, with figures like Opposition Leader Angus Taylor questioning why he was arrested in a public place, and in front of his family.

Loading...

In evidence to a Senate Estimates hearing, AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett argued the airport was the best option for a number of operational reasons.

That included information gained by war crimes investigators that Roberts-Smith could be bound overseas, which was previously disclosed in court documents.

"The individual had no known fixed abode, and the [Office of the Special Investigator] had received information that the individual was planning to relocate overseas," she said on Thursday.

Inside Ben Roberts-Smith's prosecution Once celebrated as Australia's most decorated living war hero, the looming prosecution of Ben Roberts-Smith is dividing the force.

"An operational decision was made to arrest the individual at Sydney Airport on the 7th of April, 2026."

Commissioner Barrett said airports were frequently used by police to make arrests, as people in airports were screened by security and were contained within them.

She said suggestions made in the media that the AFP wanted to arrest him in New South Wales to avoid a trial before a Queensland jury are "inaccurate".

The former SAS corporal has said he categorically denies all of the allegations. (AAP: Bianca de Marchi)

Commissioner Barrett also addressed why police did not take up an offer for Roberts-Smith to hand himself in.

"For a range of reasons, including the seriousness of the charges, which are five counts of war crime murder, and carry a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, this was determined to be an unviable option."

She said officers were aware he would be travelling with family, and additional officers were deployed to help Roberts-Smith's family after his arrest.

'Determined' to track down media leaks

Commissioner Barrett told the hearing that she intended to find out how details of the planned arrest were leaked to the media before it took place.

The leaks have been referred to the National Anti-Corruption Commission, and both the AFP and OSI have said they do not know how the details emerged.

Nine News had crews at Sydney Airport before the arrest took place, and captured vision of the arrest from inside the terminal.

"I am not just disappointed that the media outlet was there; I am determined to find out how they knew of the arrest," she said.

Media leaks ahead of Ben Roberts-Smith arrest referred to corruption commission News crews were at Sydney Airport as a plane carrying Ben Roberts-Smith landed, and captured images of his arrest from inside the terminal.

"I want to be very clear, and this is really important — if the date of the individual's arrest or other sensitive information was disclosed to anyone in the media, this could be an unauthorised disclosure.

"And in my view, anyone who disclosed that information should face consequences."

The AFP was given authorisation to make the arrest on April 1, after it was considered by the Commonwealth Department of Public Prosecutions and approved by the Attorney-General.

Operational planning then began, before Roberts-Smith was arrested on April 7.

World.title: People trapped in new housing estate traffic bottlenecks welcome funding
World.content:
For locals in Melbourne's booming outer northern suburbs the traffic issue dominates discussion like no other.

Mustafa Aljburi recently moved to the area and said driving is a daily headache.

"Every morning me and my wife will have an argument about how we go to work," he said.

He pointed out the window of his van to a line of stationary cars and trucks, in each direction, on Donnybrook Road in Kalkallo.

It is a notorious 8-kilometre single lane stretch of road where thousands of people live in housing estates to the north and south.

"I think if you video for 30 seconds it's enough," he said.

Traffic along Donnybrook Road in Melbourne's outer north is consistently bumper-to-bumper at peak hour. (ABC News: Margaret Paul)

The population of Kalkallo has boomed from about 100 people in 2001 to more than 10,000.

Council data shows traffic volumes have grown from 2,900 vehicles a day in 2017 to 35,562 vehicles a day in 2025.

The ABC went for a walk inside one of the housing estates where the line of traffic to get onto Donnybrook Road snaked back 500 meres during the morning peak.

It was moving so slowly we could walk along beside and interview people while they waited to drop their kids to school.

"Do you know how many times I leave my car in park? I just put it in park because I'm not moving, it's crazy," one resident said through their window.

Others described leaving earlier and earlier to drop children at school, or changing work hours to try to avoid peak times.

Melbourne motorist Tugce Gedik says she's often delayed by traffic jams in the city's outer north. (ABC News: Margaret Paul)

Tugce Gedik said she lives a two minute drive away, but with traffic the childcare drop off regularly blows out.

"Honestly it's really hard," she said.

"I come here in an hour and 15 minutes. It's always backed up here," she said.

Councils welcome funding, say more is needed

This month's federal and state budgets contained a combined $45 million for the next stage of upgrades to Donnybrook Road.

It includes a second bridge over the Hume Freeway and footpaths so more people can safely walk to Donnybrook train station.

The funding builds on earlier commitments to upgrade a roundabout and build a new bridge over the Kalkallo Creek.

The deputy mayor of Hume City Council, Ally Watson, lives in Kalkallo and said Donnybrook Road is a "lifeline" for thousands of people.

Cr Watson welcomed the next stage of funding but said the community needs clarity around when roadworks will happen.

Ally Watson says funding for Donnybrook Road is welcome but clarity over its rollout is needed. (ABC News: Margaret Paul)

"That is progress but really we need to see shovels in the ground. We need to see things happening for my community to believe that this is happening," she said.

Cr Watson said it's a lovely community to be part of, but they need better infrastructure.

" There's new estates popping up on Donnybrook Road every week, it feels like, so we've got new families moving in. We just can't get them in and out. "

The deputy mayor pointed to the council's advocacy strategy where four of the six projects related to local roads.

"It tells you the outer north is really doing the heavy lifting in terms of housing, supporting new communities," she said.

"But we don't have the road infrastructure, so people can't move around in the way they should be able to move around in our new communities."

Whittlesea mayor Lawrie Cox says a planned upgrade to Donnybrook Road isn't expansive enough. (ABC News: Steve Kelly)

In the neighbouring municipality Whittlesea Mayor Lawrie Cox said the planned upgrades do not go far enough.

"Donnybrook Road is already under significant strain and demand will continue to grow rapidly," he said.

"We urgently need a complete, coordinated upgrade of the full corridor so it can safely and efficiently support the communities that rely on it every day."

Call for reclassification of growth zones

The chief executive of the National Growth Areas Alliance (NGAA), Bronwen Clarke, said Donnybrook Road was emblematic of poor coordination in outer suburbs of all major Australian cities.

"It is happening every day in every outer metropolitan growth council in every Australian state and territory," she said.

National Growth Areas Alliance chief executive Bronwen Clark. (ABC News: Barrie Pullen)

Ms Clarke said housing data shows people want to live in detached homes in the outer suburbs, but the infrastructure is not there when they move in.

"It's an enormous missed opportunity because we have this capacity when new suburbs are being built to build them well," she said.

" At the moment with the housing accord we're looking only at a house. But people need more than a house. Economies need more than people living in houses. "

She welcomes a $2 billion local infrastructure fund in the federal budget, but said outer suburbs should be treated separately from metropolitan areas.

"We actually need to classify outer suburban areas as growth zones," she said.

"They need different treatment, they need different investment, and while we're grouping them in as one metro region we're going to keep up these missed connections."

Kalkallo resident Melissa Compton says locals are fed up with traffic delays. (ABC News: Margaret Paul)

A spokesperson for Federal Infrastructure Minister Catherine King described Donnybrook Road as a "vital link".

"Planning for the expanded Donnybrook Road upgrade is underway and we will continue to work with the Victorian government to deliver the project," the spokesperson said.

Design and cost works for stage two are underway and construction is expected to start in early 2028.

The Victorian upper house Liberal MP for Northern Victoria, Wendy Lovell, said the state government should have upgraded Donnybrook Road years ago.

"This is not acceptable for major estates where we have thousands of people living," she said.

"What we're seeing is people with only one road in and one road out of their estate and it is not a road to the standard to service those estates, even if there was a second entrance."

The Victorian government has been contacted by the ABC for comment.

World.title: Ex-police officer admits sharing bed but denies rape, court hears
World.content:
A former South Australian police officer says he got into bed with a woman while she was sleeping and caressed her thigh soon after she rejected his advances, but denies raping her, a court has heard.

Warning: This story includes allegations of rape that some readers may find distressing.

The woman was known to the man, who the ABC has chosen not to name to protect the identity of the alleged victim.

He is standing trial in South Australia's District Court and has previously pleaded not guilty to two counts of rape and one count of attempted rape.

The court heard the man had consumed four beers, between five and six glasses of wine, and a line of cocaine the night of the alleged incident.

The married ex-officer told the court he initiated a hug with the woman and then, in a "spontaneous" move, attempted to kiss her.

"As the hug was ending, it lasted a few seconds, I pulled her back towards me, and I attempted to kiss her on the lips," he said.

"And how did she react to that?" his defence lawyer asked.

"She immediately withdrew and said 'nope'… she walked straight past me and into the room," the man said.

The former officer has pleaded not guilty to two counts of rape and one count of attempted rape. (ABC News)

The former officer told the court he then slept in a daybed in just his "jocks" for about an hour before he woke up "shivering" due to the cold temperature.

He then went into the bedroom where the woman was sleeping primarily to "warm" himself up in bed, and also to "comfort her" after the alleged kiss.

"I climbed into the bed … I sidled up to her … and I essentially got myself into a spooning position, my body pressed against hers … with my right hand I rubbed up and down her leg, hip and torso area."

"… She appeared to be asleep."

He told the court that this went on for 30 seconds before the woman climbed out of bed with her dogs.

Upon cross-examination, the prosecution denied this series of events.

Prosecutor Karen Ingleton put forward to the man the kiss never happened and when he got into bed, he proceeded to attempt to rape and then rape the woman — something the man strenuously denied.

"[That] did not happen at all," he said.

He also said he was prescribed different medications, such as mood stabilisers for diagnoses of PTSD, anxiety, depressive mood disorder and work-related stress.

One of those, he said, was Amisulpride.

He spoke to his doctor about "a suppressed libido and ability to arouse any sexual desire and difficulty obtaining an erection" due to that medication.

The trial before Judge Ian White is continuing.

World.title: Young police officer's death raises questions about mental health support
World.content:
The mother of a NSW Police recruit who ended his life less than three months into the job has disagreed with suggestions his death was related to his work.

The young officer, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, was found dead in his locked police vehicle in western NSW in 2023.

Counsel representing the officer's girlfriend Kate Guilfoyle told an inquest into his death that it "was directly connected to his work, although it's not directly connected to the actions of any person or situation".

But the probationary constable's mother shared a different opinion in a statement to the court, saying her son had spoken about his work with enthusiasm and warmth.

"I don't believe what happened to [my son] was due to his work," she said.

"When [he] spoke about work or told us a story, his whole tone would change.

"He spoke highly of the other officers … and in his own words, he felt very welcomed."

'No-one saw it coming'

The inquest before Judge Kasey Pearce at Lidcombe Coroners Court this week examined the mental health supports available to new recruits, staff shortages at remote stations, and the process by which probationary constables were allocated to stations across the state.

It heard the young officer hoped to join the cybercrime unit and persevered through medical issues to complete his police training before being sent to a rural town more than eight hours' drive from his family and friends.

The remote posting was not one of his location preferences, and he initially attempted to find someone from his graduating cohort to swap with him.

But the court heard he ultimately accepted the allocation with the benefits and incentives it provided, including a "golden ticket" guaranteed transfer to a station of his choice once his three-year tenure was up.

His girlfriend moved with him, but the inquest heard both were caught off guard by the lack of services available in the remote town and struggled to adjust.

His colleagues described him as an enthusiastic and capable officer, who was reserved and shy at times, but a pleasure to work with and progressing at the expected rate.

Counsel assisting the coroner Christine Melis told the inquest that after four days of evidence, "there didn't appear to be any red flags" to indicate the young officer was contemplating taking his life or raised any particular concerns.

"Perhaps the greatest tragedy in this case is that no-one saw it coming," she said.

Staffing pressures and lack of resources at the remote police station were a key focus of the inquest. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Mental health battle only seen at home

But while the young officer was performing well at the job, his girlfriend told the inquest that weeks before he died, she found him slumped and crying in his computer chair, telling her he "couldn't take it anymore".

She described him as increasingly depressed, lonely and anxious, spending more time playing video games and neglecting to exercise.

The court heard that near the end of his last shift, he transferred $15,000 in three transactions to her bank account with a note saying: "I'm sorry."

His final hours included a text exchange where she told him, "Enjoy your shift babe. I love you" and he replied, "I love you too".

Two weeks before his death, the young man signed up to the NSW Police Provident Fund, which financially supports family members of officers who die on duty.

An inquest into the self-inflicted death of a new police recruit has explored mental health support in the force. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Staffing and rosters probed

A central concern raised in closing submissions was the decision to send the young officer 100 kilometres away to work a shift at a nearby police station struggling with staffing shortages.

Ms Melis described that as "a concerning matter" because ideally, a probationary constable should not be required to drive independently to complete a shift at another station.

The inquest also heard that staff shortages at his own station prevented him from always being accompanied by his assigned field training and assessment officer as required.

The inquest also examined systemic pressures, including chronic staff shortages across country NSW police commands, unpredictable rosters, and the profound isolation of remote postings.

The inquest heard NSW Police had introduced a raft of changes since the officer's death, including embedding mental health clinicians in police districts and at the police academy.

Assistant Commissioner Rashelle Conroy, who leads the Health, Safety and Wellbeing Command established in July 2024, told the inquest those changes were "part of his legacy".

Judge Pearce is expected to deliver her findings from the four-day inquest before the end of the year.

World.title: 'Scary as hell': Divers on the upcoming mission to rescue Laos villagers
World.content:
A Finnish diver at the centre of the effort to rescue a group of men in a flooded cave in central Laos has described the extraordinary moment when he found them.

Meanwhile, a South Australian diver will be landing in Laos on Friday morning to join the rescue team and says the cave holding the group looks "scary as hell".

The group entered the cave in Xaysomboun province last week to look for gold, but heavy rainfall caused a landslide and flash flooding that blocked their exit.

Despite fears about their survival, specialist divers found five men on Wednesday evening, a week after they went missing.

Vision of their discovery by Thailand-based Finnish cave diver Mikko Paasi and Thai diver Norrased Palasing was reminiscent of the extraordinary 2018 Thai cave rescue, showing the group of men huddled on a rocky shelf, smiling back at rescuers.

Loading...

Mikko Paasi, who played a role in the 2018 rescue, said he had been sleeping less than three hours a night in the lead-up to locating the group.

"That was an emotional moment [when we found them], like what are the chances? We believed they were still alive, but the odds were quite low given everything," Mr Paasi told the ABC, in an exclusive interview about the mission.

"Ascending to the final chamber where they were and seeing them sitting there all grey and all pale but in good spirits.

"They were very happy, there were tears, big smiles from both sides.

"The feeling of not giving up, and succeeding … now we are one step closer to getting them back out to their families and kids. It was overwhelming."

Mikko Paasi climbing backwards to locate the group in the Laos cave. (Supplied: Mikko Paasi)

The men becoming trapped sparked a major search and rescue effort, involving a Thai volunteer rescue group.

Mr Paasi is helping recruit an international team to help out, including South Australian diver Josh Richards, who is renowned locally for his exploration efforts navigating tight restrictions and underground passages in the Limestone Coast region.

Josh Richards will assist with rescue efforts in Laos. (ABC South East SA: Bec Whetham)

Mr Richards said his friendship with Mr Paasi, and his small stature and ability to squeeze into tight spaces, were why he was called in.

"I'm pretty scared, if I'm honest," he said.

"The stuff that Mikko has shared via video should scare anybody who watches it."

Mr Richards will land in Laos on Friday morning local time to act as a support diver on the mission.

Josh Richards squeezing through a tight restriction at Pines Cave near Tantanoola, SA. (Supplied: Josh Richards)

Diver had to 'wriggle like a worm' to reach trapped villagers

Initial reports suggested seven men had gone missing, although Mr Paasi said the group of five men said no-one else was with them.

The cave is about 125 kilometres north-east of the capital, Vientiane, in a mountainous area of the country.

Mr Paasi said the men had prepared to stay inside the mine for several days, because of the difficulty in getting in and out, but they were not prepared to be there for any longer.

Since discovering the group, Mr Paasi and Mr Palasing have been back to deliver them food and water, pulling supplies through the labyrinthine cave system.

Loading...

He said the men were about 300 metres into the extremely narrow cave, with the final 30 metres of the cave flooded in.

"If claustrophobia had a form, this would be it," Mr Paasi said.

The experienced Finnish cave diver said he had to "wriggle through like a worm" to get to the flooded chamber.

"It's a constant, super tight restriction," he said.

"I had to go through places where I had to exhale to wiggle my body through.

Mikko Paasi wades through chest-deep water in the cave system in Laos. (Supplied: Mikko Paasi)

"Moving inside the tunnels — hundreds of metres of tunnels — is done by fingertips or toe-tips.

"The diving is the same … you take a tank in your hand and you reverse into a hole that you can barely fit your chest in.

"It's a really dangerous way of diving. If something happens, you are so deep in the ground, behind such long, tight tunnels, that you're pretty much on your own."

South Australian diver called in to navigate 'smaller' caves

Even Mr Richards, who has a history of navigating difficult caves in Australia, said the system in Xaysomboun province looked intimidating.

In 2022, Mr Richards was part of a team that discovered a 400-metre extension to the Limestone Coast's second-largest known cave, and in 2025, he was part of a team that found a 100m tunnel in another prominent cave-diving spot in South Australia.

Josh Richards at the entrance to Pines Cave in South Australia. (ABC News)

"The thing that scares me the most, out of watching those videos [of the cave in Laos], is the mud walls," he told the ABC.

"It's all clay, it's all soft, it's all mud. There's not a lot holding the roof up.

"If you've seen the water that we're heading into, you can't see anything.

" It's like diving into coffee. "

Loading...

Rescuers are pursuing multiple options to extract the men from the cave, and are pumping water out in the hope the men can crawl out.

The rainy season has just begun in Laos, and storms will threaten how successfully and swiftly water can be pumped out of the tunnel.

While he will be ready and willing to help, Mr Richards was holding out hope that the men would be freed without the need for divers.

"It would be wonderful if I landed in Laos and got news that the military had managed to pump all the water out and there were five dudes who were hanging out, drinking coffee outside of the mine," he said.

"I'm not a big one for living with hope; I am going to go there and try."

'Big trouble' awaits mission if rain picks up

Getting the men out while sections are flooded will prove extremely challenging, with Mr Paasi saying members of the international team need to be "hard-headed", "slim", and "less than 70 or 60 kilograms".

"We're waiting for the next weather forecast for this area, to see exactly what we're looking at and then we will have to make a decision according to the weather," he said.

"When it starts to rain we're going to be in big trouble.

"The pumping systems are not that efficient."

Mr Richards said his involvement was only confirmed yesterday afternoon after the five people were found.

He said he spoke with his mother and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade last night about his plans.

He also texted Thai cave rescuer and former Australian of the Year Dr Richard Harris.

Loading...

"I won't repeat [his advice] but it was very good advice," he said.

"There's parallels between the two, but they're also very different situations.

"The kind of restrictions that we're going to be navigating in Laos are much smaller.

"It's part of the reason why I've been contacted."

World.title: Live: Blues hunting Women's Origin clean sweep on soaked Gold Coast
World.content:
The Women's State of Origin series wraps up on the Gold Coast, with NSW hunting a clean sweep at a rain-soaked Robina Stadium on the Gold Coast.

Follow all the action in our live blog below and tune in to our live radio coverage.

Live updates Live: Qld Maroons vs NSW Blues at Robina Stadium J By Jon Healy Collapse all posts off Sort Sort posts Latest Select an option New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Filter Posts All 22 Key Events 8 Tries 2 HALF-TIME: All square at 4-4 on the Gold Coast J By Jon Healy (Getty) 35' Queensland blows its last chance J By Jon Healy A penalty puts Queensland in great field position, but something must have gone horrible wrong with the communication on the last tackle. Chantay Kiria-Ratu gives the ball to middle forward Lillian Yarrow, who tries to manufacture a kick and just about has an air-swing. Jasmine Peters is over for the Maroons! J By Jon Healy The Maroons get a fresh set as the Blues fail to shut down the bomb from Chantay Kiria-Ratu. Then Jaime Chapman fumbles an intercept that could have easily ended in a 90-metre try. Queensland spins it right and a little shimmy from debutant Destiny Mino-Sinapati creates enough space to send Jasmine Peters over in the corner. A massive moment for Peters, who was denied thrice in Game II, including the potential game-tying try in the final seconds. The skipper gets the Blues on the board J By Jon Healy Another error, this one from Romy Teitzel, gives NSW a chance in the red zone and finally they execute. The Blues go out to their strong left side and Ivana Lolesio hugely over-commits trying to anticipate the short ball to Yasmin Meakes, but Jesse Southwell throws it out the back to Abbi Church, who pops a simple pass for Isabelle Kelly to go over untouched. 24' Queensland enforcers doing damage J By Jon Healy Brianna Clark and Lillian Yarrow have come onto the field for their first game time tonight and immediately give away back-to-back penalties for high tackles. The Maroons are clearly trying to make a statement with their defence, and now Jada Ferguson forces the error from Olivia Kernick right in front of the posts. Queensland's defence has been pretty ordinary so far tonight, but my word have the been strong without the ball. 22' The pressure tells as Fressard crashes over, but she can't get it down! J By Jon Healy The Blues get a set restart and quickly spin it left. Jesse Southwell creates the extra number out wide and they get it out to winger Jayme Fressard, who crashes over and gets up celebrating, but the replays are a bit iffy. Here comes the bunker … NO TRY. Jasmine Peters did sensationally well to make strong ball-and-all contact and force a bobble at the last moment. 19' Blues get a fresh set on the Maroons' line J By Jon Healy With Julia Robinson injured, the NSW halves keep putting Jaime Chapman into aerial contests with Shenae Ciesiolka. This time Ciesiolka comes up with the error and NSW has a full set from 10 metres out. 14' More unbelievable defence from the Maroons J By Jon Healy Jaime Chapman looks certain to score off the cross-field kick as she wins the aerial battle with Shenae Ciesiolka. Chapman comes down with the ball and spins out of Rory Owen's tackle, but Lauren Brown arrives out of nowhere to hit, stick and bring Chapman down a metre short on the last. 10' Queensland turns them away again J By Jon Healy Another handling error by Queensland puts the Maroons under the pump again, but the goal-line defence stands up and manages to force the mistake from Olivia Kernick on the left. They're defending the errors for now, but they need to stop handing the Blues the ball. 7' NSW forcing the Maroons to kick out of trouble J By Jon Healy The NSW defence is surging and Queensland is battling to get beyond its 30m line. Five-eighth Chantay Kiria-Ratu has the biggest boot in the NRLW and she's using it to great effect with early kicks trying to catch the Blues' back three napping. 5' First error of the game puts Queensland under the pump J By Jon Healy It's an inexcusable one from Keilee Joseph, who just loses her concentration for a moment as the dummy-half pass comes her way and the ball just balloons off her chest. The Blues attack from 20 metres out. 3' Early win for the debutant J By Jon Healy The first bomb goes up from Jocelyn Kelleher and just lingers for a second at its apex, but rookie fullback Destiny Mino-Sinapati sets herself under it and makes a clean grab. That will do wonders for her nerves. Meanwhile, at the other end Jayme Fressard slips and bobbles but manages to reel it in. 1' The Blues kick us off J By Jon Healy And Jessika Elliston takes the first charge in anger. Plenty of pepper in the NSW defence. They will be desperate to avoid the misery of last year's finale. The players are on the field J By Jon Healy The Blues emerge first before the Maroons, led by Lauren Brown. Two debutants in the Queensland line-up — fullback Destiny Mino-Sinapati and Lillian Yarrow off the bench. About last night … J By Jon Healy There was plenty of drama in the men's series opener last night. A send-off, bunker controversies, a remarkable comeback … it was frankly, almost too much. Maroons let 20-0 lead slip in Origin I after Kalyn Ponga sent off late What happened last year? J By Jon Healy (Supplied: NRL.com) From that image, you might think 2025 was a miserable series for NSW, but it really wasn't. Just like this year, the Blues wrapped up the shield in the first two games, but captain Isabelle Kelly was left in tears after the dead rubber. Ultimately, NSW lost Game III by four points after Kelly dove in untouched for a try, but only grounded the ball on top of her own arm and had the try taken off her. It soured the series victory for her as she lamented letting her teammates down even after lifting the shield and celebrating with them. How has the series shaken out thus far? J By Jon Healy (Getty) Despite NSW having a dominant team on paper yet again in this series and winning it inside two games, the margins have been exceedingly tight. Queensland was on top in the first contest in Newcastle, leading 6-0 at half-time before an equaliser by Ellie Johnston. Scores remained tied until the final few minutes when a Jesse Southwell field goal separated them, and Jess Sergis crossed right on full-time as NSW's lead blew all the way out to 11-6. Another rain-affected game in Brisbane came down to the final play, with Jasmine Peters's boot skimming the sideline on the last play as the Blues held on for a 14-10 win. LATE MAIL: Lenarduzzi and Dodd in jersey 18 J By Jon Healy Both Queensland and NSW are 1-17 tonight, Here are the full team lists: (NRL.com) Triple blow for Maroons J By Jon Healy If you were asked to name the five most important players for the Maroons, Tamika Upton and Julia Robinson would definitely be amongst them, and Makenzie Weale may well have got a mention as well. But for Game III, with Queensland once again desperately trying to avoid being swept, fullback and captain Upton, dynamic winger Robinson and influential middle forward Weale are all missing. Already without the retired Ali Brigginshaw and injured Tarryn Aiken for the series, it is the sort of blow I don't think the Maroons can overcome. Maroons hit with triple injury blow as Blues look for whitewash Show more posts

World.title: Bleijie backs private school’s move to clear bushland as koala spotted
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEnvironmental protection Bleijie backs private school’s move to clear bushland as koala spotted Cameron Atfield May 28, 2026 — 8:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland’s deputy premier has defended his decision to allow a bayside private school to clear bushland for new sport fields, a day after GPS tracked another koala entering the area, which was already being cleared. Protests have been held outside Ormiston College since Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie green-lit the destruction of contested koala habitat to make way for the expansion of the private school’s sporting fields last week. “Leave koalas alone” has been graffitied on the college’s welcome sign, and at least one person, former Greens candidate Kristie Lockhart, has been arrested for jumping a fence. Graffiti outside Ormiston College. Facebook College principal Michael Hornby told media this week that the school was adhering to strict conditions, denying the area was a koala habitat.



Redland City Council has disputed the ecological report on which Hornby relied to reach that conclusion – although it said it supported the project in principle. GPS tracking has shown Leaf in the Ormiston College bushland being cleared. Redlands Koala Action Group On Thursday, the Redlands Koala Action Group reported a GPS-tracked koala named Leaf had moved on to the Ormiston College site overnight. Leaf survived a car strike that left her blind in one eye and separated from her missing joey last year, and was released into bushland after months of rehabilitation. “This loss of this significant mapped core koala habitat is absolutely devastating to Leaf and the other koalas that call this area home and makes a mockery of the state government’s new koala strategy,” Redlands Koala Action Group president Debbie Pointing said.



“It’s been heartbreaking for the community to witness century-old trees that we know are regularly utilised by Leaf and other koalas simply being cut down for sporting ovals is morally wrong.” Related Article Brisbane development Private school given go-ahead to cut down koala habitat for new ovals Speaking at Howard Smith Wharves on Thursday afternoon, Bleijie defended his decision and said it was based on independent advice from the State Development and Planning Department. “You could complain about every MID [ministerial infrastructure designation] that every former Labor government had done,” he said. “The planning ministers do the infrastructure designations all the time – it’s nothing new, and that is simply what we’ve done in this case.



“And I’ve seen the comments from the principal – I think they were very good comments – and I’ve also seen again protesters illegally trespassing, attacking a college, a school in that area, and graffitiing the outside of it. “We’ll treat everyone respectfully, but people have to abide by the laws and Ormiston College is applying and abiding by the laws in place.” Protesters outside the college this week. Queensland Koala Conservation Collective - Facebook Redland City Council denied a similar application from Ormiston College to add an oval and a slew of buildings around the campus in 2021, but the school took new plans directly to the state government last April. A petition to Bleijie urging him to reject the plan, which would remove 652 mature trees, attracted 8300 signatures.



Pointing said Leaf’s movements were a clear demonstration of how important the site was to the local koala population. “Then to hear yesterday the college principal say it’s not habitat, and any koalas on the site are lost, is sheer ignorance and denial,” she said. Comment has been sought from Ormiston College. Pointing said the Koala Action Group had asked the federal government to call in the project and overrule Bleijie’s decision. A spokesperson for the Federal Environment Department said while they were aware of the Ormiston College project, they had not received a referral.



They added that it was the school’s responsibility to refer the proposal for assessment, “if a significant impact on matters of national environmental significance is likely”. “In this instance, the proponent is aware of their obligations under national environmental law, and a self-assessment was undertaken and included in the Queensland government Ministerial Infrastructure Designation approval documents,” the spokesperson said. World.title: Football Australia just posted a record loss. Gianni Infantino hailed it ‘a wonderful year’
World.content:
SportSoccerFootball Australia Football Australia just posted a record loss. Gianni Infantino hailed it ‘a wonderful year’ Emma Kemp May 28, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It took almost three full hours, but the cavalry finally came. For two hours and 40 minutes, Football Australia’s annual general meeting was the unfortunate host of a $15.3 million dissection. Questions were asked about the unprecedented loss posted for 2025, and then asked again in different ways in the hope of eliciting clearer answers. Grievances were aired about the sorry state of the code’s finances and the governance missteps that got it there, and assurances sought that a clear path forward had now been charted (FA said it expected to lose $5 million in 2026 but aimed to break even in 2027). Football Australia chairman Anter Isaac addresses Thursday’s AGM. Getty Images for Football Australia By the time two of the three nominees vying to fill the governing body’s three available board positions had failed to receive the required number of votes, there was a creeping sense nothing and nobody could rescue a day already destined to be dark. But then re-elected FA chair Anter Isaac said something about a video message coming through from FIFA. “I haven’t seen the video, so it’s a bit risky,” Isaac added. Moments later, the bright smile of FIFA president Gianni Infantino beamed up on the big screen to tell all the unhappy souls in the room that everything would be all right.



“Dear chairman,” he began. “Dear Anter,” he continued, also addressing the chairman. “Dear Football Australia members, dear friends and colleagues from Football Australia. It is my great pleasure to address your 23rd annual general meeting and to congratulate you on a wonderful year of firsts, of milestones, and of growth, in your beautiful country.” Infantino gushed about “the great work done by President Anter Isaac and Football Australia to continue building and supporting football in the years following that beautiful tournament” (“that beautiful tournament” was the 2023 Women’s World Cup – the one that was meant to have FA rolling in cash by now). Fantasy land: FIFA president Gianni Infantino. Getty Images Infantino proved his Australian football nous by praising the inaugural Australian Championship for “helping to take giant leaps in reuniting old soccer and new football – as you say in your country” and name-dropping South Melbourne as inaugural OFC Pro League runners-up. And, with the Australian flag draped behind him, he wished the Socceroos luck at the upcoming World Cup: “the biggest and most inclusive ever”. In a way, Infantino’s malapropos cameo was so very Australian football. Because who would be better to improve bad optics than a guy internationally renowned for his capacity to create them? He did, at the very least, take FA’s reported “toxic” working environment and turn it into toxic positivity. The pre-recorded five-minute-and-four-second video, which Isaac said was not planned or expected, was an entertaining – if slightly gaslighty – reprieve from the rest.



And the rest was a lot. It was the unpacking of FA’s 2025 financial results: that record $15m loss which followed the record $8 million loss of 2024 and forced the organisation to cut 20 per cent of its workforce. And the examination of how all-time-high revenues of almost $140m were gobbled away by costs relating to now-resolved disputes with the Australian Professional Leagues, not to mention the $14m rise in employee and team benefit expenses. Isaac, who answered questions alongside FA’s chief financial officer Adam Santo and chief executive Martin Kugeler, said recommendations from a board-initiated travel and expenditure review – one of numerous reviews conducted – had been fulfilled by the end of 2025. But he was pressed on the $810,000 payment to former board member Jaclyn Lee-Joe for services in relation to FA’s launch of the PlayFootball 2.0 registration platform. Football Australia chief executive Martin Kugeler last week announced a $15.3m annual loss. Getty Images for Football Australia “What was the governance process that was put around that, for her to step off and then be paid that and contracted to deliver that piece of work?” asked Professional Football Australia chief executive, Beau Busch, from a remote video call. Isaac answered: “The payment that was paid to her was a decision that the board made. It did inform Congress FRAC. It did go through FRAC process – the board Finance, Risk, and Audit Committee – as well.” Shortly thereafter, Football NSW chairman Gilbert Lorquet got to his feet in the room to pose a follow-up question on behalf of some unnamed state federations. “Some members are asking ... the point about FRAC,” he said. “Some of the member feds are actually questioning the point you mentioned around discussing [the] Jaclyn Lee-Joe payment. Can you point out when and the hours it was discussed with and agreed by FRAC? And this is coming from someone on FRAC, by the way, from the member feds.”



When Isaac responded to say he did not “have the emails with me now but we’ll find that, we’ll chase that up”, Lorquet pushed further. “Just in transparency … to say that we’re angry is probably an understatement … this is an AICD case study waiting to happen. I think having a board member sitting there and then knowing if there’s agreements set up previously that they will eventually be paid, I think it’s actually a huge disaster. I think addressing and owning that is important. Once you own that, what is the plan going forward to ensure that those things don’t happen? Because I know there’s another director on the line who’s actually being caught up in a similar situation. It’s not the first time.” Related Article Australian soccer Football Australia to post $15.3 million loss as full scale of financial troubles revealed Isaac acknowledged the issue as “a source of frustration for all of us”. “It’s something that the board is very strong on ensuring never happens again,” he said. “It happened unfortunately 10 years ago with another director, and history repeated. I mean, the systems and the policies are very clear about directors not being paid while they’re serving.” Equally frustrating might have been the exponential shrinking of board candidates to fill the three vacant seats. Three of the initial six, which included Socceroos great Mark Schwarzer, withdrew before the ballot, leaving three contenders in Paul Bittar, Jon Sutton and Mark Goodrick – all nominated by A-Leagues clubs. But neither Sutton nor Goodrick were deemed worthy directors by voters, the bulk of which are state federations, meaning the meeting closed with two vacancies.



FA will seek to fill those immediately and, given Thursday’s amendment to the constitution in line with Australian Sports Commission requirements (as demanded to remain eligible for ASC funding) to stipulate an even gender split, could well be women. Rachel Wiseman was also appointed deputy chair. In perhaps more encouraging news, chief financial officer Adam Santo said FA was not relying on the Socceroos making a deep World Cup run to break even in 2027. He was also adamant FA did not take out a bank facility despite apparent mentions of it in the report. And Isaac later, under heavy questioning, repeatedly stated, “We’ve written off nothing for the APL” as part of their confidential settlement. Both he and Kugeler spoke of uncomfortable truths during their respective addresses, with Kugeler lamenting that FA had been “too internally focused” and needed to listen to what fans and participants want and need. Isaac’s pitch involved three prerequisites for a successful future. “We are deeply focused on and committed to delivering, alignment, sustainability and excellence,” he said. Then Infantino materialised and some must have wondered: what in the name of alignment, sustainability and excellence is he doing here? World.title: Don’t fence our schools in. Where else will the children (and grown-ups) play?
World.content:
PoliticsNSWSchools Opinion Don’t fence our schools in. Where else will the children (and grown-ups) play? Jen George Academic, urban planning expert May 28, 2026 — 7:30pm

May 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When I was growing up in the 1980s, schools routinely opened their grounds to local communities. Buildings might have been locked, but playgrounds and ovals were open on weekends and after-hours. The Rose Bay Secondary College neighbourhood lockout, as reported in this masthead, shows the NSW Department of Education is fencing itself off from deep, long-held community sentiment. This is not the first time a fence has been erected around a school’s open space; there are almost 1400 state schools in NSW with security fencing. And independent and Catholic schools have come under pressure to open their grounds to the wider community. For many principals, parents and teachers, the barrier offers relief. For residents, it feels unfair. Until the community was locked out, Joseph Kantor loved to play on the fields of Rose Bay Secondary College in North Bondi. Janie Barrett Shared open spaces reflected an era shaped by ideas about liveable, people-centred cities, especially those advanced by the late American-Canadian urban thinker Jane Jacobs. Jacobs argued that active, shared public spaces, supported by natural surveillance and “eyes on the street”, helped create safe and inclusive communities. That philosophy once felt deeply Australian. We have long resisted the idea that beaches, parks or sporting fields should belong exclusively to any particular group. Open space was for sharing. Anyone could join a game of cricket on the oval. Strangers became teammates.



Today, however, many schools are increasingly fenced off from the communities around them. Security concerns are often used to justify fortress-like barriers, but the evidence does not necessarily support that approach. Research suggests that opening green space to the public can improve safety rather than diminish it. The New York-based architect and urban planner Oscar Newman’s “defensible space theory” emphasised establishing clarity around public, semi-public and private spaces, including citizens enhancing security with their eyes on these spaces, and thoughtful design over heavy, physical barriers. Related Article Sorry, your browser doesn't support embedded videos. Exclusive

Education Top private schools face pressure to open grounds to public students More recent research from the University of Melbourne examines the subject in a book called Schools as Community Hubs: Building ‘More than a School’ for Community Benefit. Several authors argue that excessive fencing can weaken schools’ relationships with their surrounding communities and create unwelcoming environments. Among the authors is architect and researcher Jamileh Jahangiri, the founder of the Sydney-based Studio Orsi,who argues that safe schools are best achieved through collaboration among students, parents, teachers and local communities. Passive security measures – thoughtful design, visibility, clear public messaging and expectations, and active use of space – can be more effective than high fences and locked gates. This is because Australians often overestimate crime risks even as crime rates have fallen. In that context, the rush to fence schools appears to be driven as much by fear, liability concerns and institutional control as by evidence.



Schools owe a duty of care to the public under common law. In the event of injury to a member of the local community, there is a risk of legal liability, which can be reduced by installing a fence and a locked gate. Alternatively, this risk can be addressed by removing foreseeable hazards, conducting regular maintenance, installing cameras, posting a “use at your own risk” sign, and maintaining insurance cover. The deeper issue at play here is the common good – the best possible outcome for the greatest number of people. A gated-community mentality works against that principle. When publicly funded schools close themselves off from surrounding neighbourhoods, they diminish opportunities for connection, recreation and shared ownership of local space. Related Article Private schools The north shore school that has closed its grounds to the public This trend extends beyond government schools. Across Australian cities, universities, churches, golf courses, neighbourhoods and independent schools have increasingly restricted access to land and facilities that were once more open. In many cases, such as Shore School’s playing fields, which cover a whopping nine hectares in Northbridge, long-existing community access has been curtailed over the past decade. It is not driven by hostility to the surrounding community’s wishes but by safeguarding concerns for students and buildings, liability and legislative requirements. One important example is section 83C of the Education Act 1990 (NSW), introduced by amendments in 2014 regarding governing not-for-profit, non-government schools. The provision was designed to ensure that government funding supported education rather than private gain. Yet in practice, it has often discouraged schools from sharing facilities freely, except on market terms.



For generations, schools shared ovals, pools, laboratories, equipment and facilities with neighbouring schools and community groups. These arrangements saved money, strengthened relationships and fostered interaction across sectors and socioeconomic backgrounds. Sharing was accepted as part of community life. It extended beyond facilities to include events, programs and collaborative learning opportunities. Related Article City life The Sydney school oval, the two-metre fence and the $585,000 demand After section 83C took effect, many informal partnerships weakened. What was intended to protect against misuse of public funding also created barriers to generosity and practical co-operation. The result has been a gradual erosion of goodwill and co-operation between state, independent, and Catholic schools and their local communities. To find space-sharing compromises, some recent examples stand out as exceptional rather than the norm. Notable are the community fluid zones on the ground floor of the Green Square Public School, senior students at St Andrew’s Cathedral School integrating with city users to share public space on a normal school day, and the recently implemented Share Our Space program, which mostly addresses public schools sharing their space during holiday periods. The local community has a legitimate expectation of sharing the open space at Rose Bay Secondary College and, indeed, at independent and Catholic schools. In the spirit of the common good, schools and other institutions should share open spaces whenever it is safe and practical. Dr Jen George is a senior lecturer at Charles Sturt University and an adviser to school communities. Her PhD was in urban planning and community governance.

World.title: Patients are waiting 1460 days for routine appointments. Authorities think AI can fix it
World.content:
NationalVictoriaHealthcare Patients are waiting 1460 days for routine appointments. Authorities think AI can fix it Henrietta Cook May 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Victorians are waiting up to four years to access specialist care in the state’s public hospitals, triggering a state government overhaul that will create regional waitlists and use AI to flag urgent cases. Under the changes, which have been outlined in a new Department of Health report, more specialist appointments would be shifted to nurses to take pressure off doctors. Lavengamalie Malagaoma’s son Michael was left waiting for years for specialist care to deal with a hearing problem. Simon Schluter Review appointments deemed unnecessary would also be cut to improve access for patients in greater need, and virtual care would be expanded. The plan is a response to an unprecedented influx of patients seeking public specialist care, driven by the cost-of-living crisis and soaring private doctors’ fees.



The report highlighted the case of a four-year-old who waited more than 12 months for an ear, nose and throat assessment, while falling behind in their development. Rural patients spoke of having to drive five hours for an appointment, only to face carpark fees of up to $70. Health Minister Harriet Shing said too many Victorians were waiting too long or struggling to navigate the complex system. Health Minister Harriet Shing says the changes will reduce delays for patients in need. Joe Armao “That’s why this reform is vital – it will mean quicker access, clearer communication, and more options for patients and their families,” she said. Rising fees for private specialists – which grew by 73 per cent between 2010 and 2025 – and the cost-of-living crisis have pushed more patients into the public system.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Out of control’ specialist fees will be Labor’s next health priority This has led to a surge in demand, with referrals to specialist care in public hospitals increasing by an average of 460,000 per year between 2020/21 and 2024/25, while appointments rose by 250,000 per year. While most patients requiring urgent appointments were seen swiftly, some patients waited up to 1460 days, or four years, for a routine appointment at a vascular clinic. “Extended wait times are stressful and worrying for patients and can increase the risk of conditions becoming more complex and needing even more intensive and expensive care, including admissions to hospital,” the report said. The report also identified waste: 11 per cent of public specialist appointments (600,000 per year) were not attended.



Professor Ben Thomson, the Department of Health’s chief surgical adviser, said there had been little reform in outpatient clinics over the past 80 years. “Pockets of innovation and reform are happening in Victoria, but nothing centrally coordinated at present,” he said. He hopes the changes improve wait times and access for patients. He is particularly interested in the proposal to boost access to virtual care and allow patients to decide when and if they need a review appointment. Only one in five specialist appointments are for new patients, with the remainder reserved for review appointments. He said many of these review appointments were booked by default, and some were unnecessary.



For parents caught in the middle of these delays, the wait can be agonising. Lavengamalie Malagaoma became concerned about her son Michael’s hearing when he was two years old. He had constant ear infections and wasn’t responding to his name. Michael’s hearing improved after he was referred to a clinic through Sunshine Hospital’s emergency department. Simon Schluter The mother-of-six from Kings Park in Melbourne’s north-west took him to a local hearing clinic and he was told he had a blockage that needed to be seen by an ENT specialist. A referral was sent to the ENT, but four years passed, and the family never heard anything. “It was frustrating,” she said. “He wouldn’t respond, he wouldn’t listen. It was because he couldn’t hear. He couldn’t sleep because he was crying.”



About two years ago, Michael’s ear worsened and after he was taken to Sunshine Hospital’s emergency department, he was referred to their Audiology Advanced Practice Paediatric Ear (AAPPEAR) Clinic. The service employs audiologists who conduct diagnostic assessments of children’s ears. Some children are discharged without needing to see an ENT specialist, while others are referred for routine or urgent appointments. Michael was swiftly seen by the clinic’s audiologists, who referred him to an ENT who recommended grommets. The grommets were placed in the now eight-year-old’s ears about a year ago. “He can hear better,” Malagaoma said. “His confidence, friendships and learning has improved.” The recent state budget included $16 million to deliver 45,000 more specialist clinic appointments for children and young people.



Editor's pick Exclusive

Hospitals Booted from hospital and dumped on the street: Patients on secret blacklist being refused treatment It also included $8 million to create and pilot a new service for GPs and patients to get specialist advice without the need for a referral. Associate Professor David Fuller, chair of Paediatric Clinical Network, said it was common for children with learning, behaviour and development issues to wait more than 18 months for an initial assessment. “It is challenging for clinicians when you get referrals and you can’t see the patients any earlier,” said Fuller, who is also a paediatrician at Barwon Health and a member of the blueprint’s expert advisory group. “You know the impact of an untreated condition can be long-term.”



His health services recently started publishing wait times for clinics so patients have more transparency. He said the blueprint would help maximise existing resources while redesigning the system so it worked better for patients. World.title: AFL LIVE: Returning Jack Gunston teaching St Kilda skipper a lesson in Marvel Stadium mauling
World.content:
Saints utility Sam Flanders has left Marvel Stadium at a hush after appearing to injure his achilles.

Flanders, who arrived at the Saints from the Suns, has become a fixture on half-back and he was in full flight when he leapt for the ball, landed and immediately appeared in discomfort.

Sam Flanders of the Saints. AFL Photos via Getty Images

He got a handball off but then crashed to the ground and couldn’t walk off the ground, needing trainers to almost carry him.

Everyone hopes it is not an achilles but it certainly looks like an achilles as no one was around him when he hurt himself.
